title: Worked t-tests: sugar bars, two classes, MBA sections and pulse rates
summary: The deck's worked one-sample (sugar in energy bars), independent two-sample (Class A vs Class B) and paired (pulse before and after training) t-tests, plus the MBA sections practice task.

chunks.heading: One-sample t-test: sugar in energy bars
chunks.explanation_md:
**Problem:** a dietician says the average sugar in an energy bar should be **15g**. You sample **10 bars**: **mean = 14g**, **standard deviation = 2g**. Is there evidence that the mean sugar is **different from 15g** at **α = 0.05**?

*Different from* means a **two-tailed** test: the null hypothesis is that the mean is 15g, the alternative that it is not.

**Calculation:**

t = (14 − 15) / (2/√10) = −1/0.632 ≈ **−1.58**

**Degrees of freedom:** df = **9**.

**Critical t** (two-tailed, α = 0.05): **±2.685**.

**Decision:** |t| = 1.58 is smaller than the critical value, so **fail to reject the null hypothesis**. The sample does not give enough evidence that the mean sugar differs from 15g.
chunks.exam_line: Sugar bars: t = (14 − 15)/(2/√10) = −1/0.632 ≈ −1.58, df = 9, critical ±2.685; |t| is smaller, so fail to reject the null hypothesis.

chunks.heading: Independent two-sample t-test: Class A vs Class B
chunks.explanation_md:
**Problem:** compare test scores between two classes.
- **Class A:** n = 15, mean = 78, SD = 10
- **Class B:** n = 14, mean = 85, SD = 8

**Step 1: Pooled SD.**

sp = √[((14)(10²) + (13)(8²)) / 27] = √[(1400 + 832) / 27] = √82.96 ≈ **9.1**

(14 is n1 − 1, 13 is n2 − 1 and 27 is n1 + n2 − 2.)

**Step 2: Compute t.**

t = (78 − 85) / (9.1 √(1/15 + 1/14)) = −7 / (9.1 × 0.38) = −7/3.46 ≈ **−2.02**

**Degrees of freedom** = 15 + 14 − 2 = **27**.

**Critical t** (two-tailed, α = 0.05) ≈ **±2.373**.

**Decision:** |t| = 2.02 is smaller than the critical value, so **fail to reject the null hypothesis**.
chunks.exam_line: Two classes: sp = √[(1400 + 832)/27] ≈ 9.1; t = −7/3.46 ≈ −2.02; df = 27; critical ±2.373; fail to reject the null hypothesis.

chunks.heading: Paired t-test: pulse rate before and after training
chunks.explanation_md:
**Problem:** a fitness trainer wants to see if a training program **reduces pulse rate**. **6 clients:** before (72, 75, 70, 80, 78, 77), after (70, 76, 69, 78, 76, 75).

**Set-up:** n = 6 clients. Differences (Before − After): **2, −1, 1, 2, 2, 2**. Mean difference **d̄ = 1.33**. Standard deviation of differences **sd = 1.211**.

**Step 1: Hypotheses.**
- H0: the program has **no effect** or does not reduce pulse rate: **H0: μd = 0**
- H1: the program **reduces** pulse rate: **H1: μd > 0**

**Step 2: t-statistic.**

t = (d̄ − μ0) / (sd/√n) = (1.33 − 0) / (1.211/√6) = 1.33/0.494 ≈ **2.69**

**Step 3: Degrees of freedom.** df = n − 1 = 6 − 1 = **5**.

**Step 4: Critical value and p-value.** One-tailed, α = 0.05, df = 5: critical t ≈ **2.571**. Calculated t = 2.69 is larger, so **reject the null hypothesis**. The one-tailed **p-value is about 0.021**, less than 0.05.

**Step 5: Conclusion.** There is **statistically significant evidence at the 5% level** that the training program **reduces pulse rate**.
chunks.exam_line: Pulse: differences 2, −1, 1, 2, 2, 2; d̄ = 1.33, sd = 1.211; t = 1.33/0.494 ≈ 2.69, df = 5; one-tailed critical 2.571, p ≈ 0.021; reject H0: the program reduces pulse rate.

questions.stem: A dietician says the average sugar content in an energy bar should be 15g. A sample of 10 bars has mean 14g and standard deviation 2g. Test at α = 0.05 whether the mean sugar differs from 15g.
questions.model_answer_md:
This is a **one-sample t-test**, two-tailed because the question asks about a difference.

**Hypotheses:** H0: μ = 15g; H1: μ ≠ 15g.

**Test statistic:**
- t = (x̄ − μ0) / (s/√n) = (14 − 15) / (2/√10)
- √10 ≈ 3.162, so 2/√10 ≈ **0.632**
- t = −1/0.632 ≈ **−1.58**

**Degrees of freedom:** df = 10 − 1 = **9**.

**Critical value:** two-tailed at α = 0.05, the t table (df 9, 0.025 column) gives **±2.685**.

**Decision:** |t| = 1.58 < 2.685, so **fail to reject H0**. There is not enough evidence that the mean sugar differs from 15g.

questions.stem: Describe how you would carry out the deck's practice task of comparing the three sections of MBA-I year in their QTM MST using independent two-sample t-tests.
questions.model_answer_md:
The deck asks for an independent two-sample t-test, with the data in Tutorial 2. The method copies the Class A vs Class B example.

- **Pair the sections:** an independent t-test compares **two** groups at a time, so compare the sections two by two.
- **Step 1, pooled SD:** sp = √[((n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²) / (n1 + n2 − 2)].
- **Step 2, t:** t = (x̄1 − x̄2) / (sp √(1/n1 + 1/n2)).
- **Step 3, df:** n1 + n2 − 2.
- **Step 4, decide:** compare |t| with the critical t from the table; if |t| is larger, reject H0 of equal means.

The sections are separate groups of students, which is why the independent (unpaired) test fits.

questions.stem: Explain why the sugar bar example uses a one-sample t-test while the two-class example uses an independent two-sample t-test.
questions.model_answer_md:
The choice depends on what is being compared.

- **Sugar bars: one-sample t-test.** One sample of bars is compared with a **specific value**, the dietician's **15g**. The one-sample test compares a single group's mean with a known or hypothesised mean.
- **Two classes: independent two-sample t-test.** Two separate groups, **Class A and Class B**, are compared with each other. The groups are **unrelated**, so the independent (unpaired) test is used.

One group against a number needs the one-sample test; two unrelated groups need the independent test.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to compare test scores between two classes. Class A: n = 15, mean = 78, SD = 10. Class B: n = 14, mean = 85, SD = 8. Test at α = 0.05 whether the mean scores differ, showing full working.
questions.model_answer_md:
Two unrelated classes are compared, so we use the **independent two-sample t-test** (equal variances assumed).

**Hypotheses:** H0: μA = μB; H1: μA ≠ μB (two-tailed).

**Step 1: Pooled SD.**
- sp = √[((n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²) / (n1 + n2 − 2)]
- = √[((14)(10²) + (13)(8²)) / 27] = √[(1400 + 832) / 27] = √(2,232/27)
- 2,232/27 ≈ 82.67, so **sp ≈ 9.09 ≈ 9.1**

**Step 2: Compute t.**
- √(1/15 + 1/14) = √(0.0667 + 0.0714) = √0.1381 ≈ **0.372**
- Denominator = 9.1 × 0.372 ≈ **3.38**
- t = (78 − 85) / 3.38 = −7/3.38 ≈ **−2.07**
- (The slide rounds the square root to 0.38 and prints t ≈ −2.02; the decision is the same.)

**Step 3: Degrees of freedom.** df = 15 + 14 − 2 = **27**.

**Step 4: Critical value.** Two-tailed at α = 0.05, the t table (df 27, 0.025 column) gives **±2.373**.

**Step 5: Decision.** |t| ≈ 2.07 (or 2.02 on the slide) is **less than 2.373**, so **fail to reject H0**.

**Conclusion:** although Class B's mean is 7 marks higher, the difference is **not statistically significant** at the 5% level, so we cannot say the two classes perform differently.

rubric.point: Independent t-test chosen; H0 equal means, two-tailed

questions.stem: A fitness trainer wants to see if a training program reduces pulse rate. Six clients' pulse rates are: before (72, 75, 70, 80, 78, 77) and after (70, 76, 69, 78, 76, 75). Test at α = 0.05 using the appropriate t-test, showing full working.
questions.model_answer_md:
The same six clients are measured before and after, so the **paired t-test** is used.

**Step 1: Hypotheses.**
- H0: the program has no effect or does not reduce pulse rate: **μd = 0**
- H1: the program reduces pulse rate: **μd > 0** (one-tailed, with d = before − after)

**Step 2: Differences.** 2, −1, 1, 2, 2, 2.
- d̄ = 8/6 ≈ **1.33**
- Squared deviations from 1.33 sum to about 7.33; 7.33/(6 − 1) ≈ 1.467; **sd = √1.467 ≈ 1.211**

**Step 3: t statistic.**
- t = (d̄ − μ0) / (sd/√n) = (1.33 − 0) / (1.211/√6)
- √6 ≈ 2.449, so 1.211/2.449 ≈ **0.494**
- t = 1.33/0.494 ≈ **2.69**

**Step 4: Degrees of freedom.** df = n − 1 = 6 − 1 = **5**.

**Step 5: Critical value and p-value.** One-tailed at α = 0.05, the t table (df 5, 0.05 column) gives **2.571**. The slide gives a one-tailed **p-value of about 0.021**.

**Step 6: Decision.** t = 2.69 > 2.571, and p ≈ 0.021 < 0.05, so **reject H0**.

**Conclusion:** there is **statistically significant evidence at the 5% level** that the training program **reduces pulse rate**.

rubric.point: Paired t-test because same clients pre and post
Reject H0: program reduces pulse rate
